books.title: Whose Tracks Are These?
books.art_why: Animal tracks and the animals shown exist in the real world and can be photographed.

pages.text: Animal Visitors How do we know whether an animal has visited a place? One way we know is because it may leave tracks, or marks in the soil. Tracks show where the animal’s body has touched the ground. Let’s find out who has visited us today!
pages.brief: A close view of soil outdoors shows clear animal tracks and marks pressed into the ground. The tracks show where an animal’s body has touched the soil. The scene suggests a place an animal may have visited, ready for someone to wonder who came by.

pages.text: Large Animals A large animal that likes honey made these tracks. This animal is a good climber. It has strong claws for digging up plants, and it eats animals, too. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: A set of large animal tracks is pressed into soft soil near a tree with a honeycomb high up. The animal that made them likes honey, is a good climber, and has strong claws for digging up plants. It also eats animals.

pages.text: A black bear made these tracks. Black bears sleep all winter and wake up hungry in the spring.
pages.brief: A black bear stands beside the tracks it made in soft soil. It is in a spring woodland, awake and hungry after sleeping all winter. Green plants and trees show the spring season around the bear.

pages.text: A large animal with hooves made these tracks. This animal can eat ten pounds of leaves, bark, and twigs each day. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: A set of large hoofed tracks is pressed into soil beside low plants and tree bark. Leaves, bark, and twigs lie nearby on the ground. The animal that made the tracks can eat ten pounds of these each day.

pages.text: A deer made these tracks. Male deer grow antlers in the spring and shed them in late winter. Baby deer have spots that disappear when they grow up.
pages.brief: A deer stands beside the tracks it made in soft ground. In the woodland nearby, a male deer has antlers and a baby deer has spots, with leaves and twigs scattered on the soft ground.

pages.text: A large, strong cat made these tracks. This hunter runs fast and jumps far. It eats other animals, such as deer, birds, and rabbits. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: A large, strong cat moves through a woodland, leaving a set of tracks in the soft soil. This hunter runs fast and jumps far. Nearby are deer, birds, and rabbits, animals the cat also eats.

pages.text: A mountain lion made these tracks. Adult mountain lions live alone most of the time. Babies must learn to hunt before they can leave their mothers.
pages.brief: A mountain lion stands beside the tracks it made in the soil of a wooded area, alone as adult mountain lions usually are. A baby mountain lion with its mother practices hunting before it can leave her.

pages.text: Small Animals A smart bird made these tracks. It has a curved beak and sharp claws. It hunts at night and eats many kinds of animals. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: A small bird with a curved beak and sharp claws stands near the tracks it made in the soil. The smart bird hunts at night and eats many kinds of animals in the dark night.

pages.text: An owl made these tracks. It has large yellow eyes and can see well in the dark. It makes a noise called a hoot.
pages.brief: An owl with large yellow eyes stands near the tracks it made in the soil at night. It can see well in the dark, and it makes a noise called a hoot. The owl’s tracks are clear in the soil.

pages.text: A small animal made these tracks. Its tail made the line between the footprints. This animal must run very fast to escape being eaten. Can you guess who it is?
pages.brief: A set of tiny footprints is pressed into soft soil, with a thin line running between them made by a small animal’s tail. The small animal must run very fast to escape from being eaten.

pages.text: A mouse made these tracks. Mice are food for owls, snakes, and other animals. But this one got away!
pages.brief: A small mouse stands beside the tiny tracks and tail line it made in the soft soil. It has escaped from animals that eat mice, such as owls and snakes. This mouse got away safely.

pages.text: Whose these? Many Kinds of Tracks Each kind of animal has its own special tracks. Look for tracks when you are in nature. Have fun finding out who has been visiting!
pages.brief: Many different kinds of animal tracks are pressed into soil and mud in a nature scene, each with its own special shape. The ground shows footprints from more than one animal, inviting a look at who has been visiting.

books.title: Dogs at Work
books.art_why: Working dogs, handlers and real places can all be photographed today.

pages.text: Introduction Dogs are not just pets. Some of them have jobs! Dogs learn fast. They hear and smell really well. Dogs can do jobs that people can’t.
pages.brief: Several working dogs with their handlers in a bright outdoor setting. One dog stands alert with ears pricked, another lowers its nose to the ground, showing dogs that are workers and not only pets, quick to learn and keen in hearing and smell.

pages.text: Service and Therapy Dogs Some dogs help people feel calm. These dogs are therapy dogs. Therapy dogs can comfort people who are sick.
pages.brief: A therapy dog lies quietly beside a person resting in bed, head close to the person's hand, in a calm, softly lit room. The dog's relaxed body and gentle nearness show comfort being given to someone who is sick.

pages.text: Other dogs help people with disabilities. These dogs are service dogs. Some help people who can’t see or hear well. Others pick up items and pull wheelchairs.
pages.brief: A service dog leads a person who cannot see along a pavement, harness taut. Nearby another dog picks up a dropped item in its mouth, and a third dog pulls a wheelchair, showing dogs helping people with different disabilities.

pages.text: Dogs have a of smell. Some can smell owner is about to be sick. They warn them to take medicine.
pages.brief: At home, a dog lifts its head and sniffs closely near its owner, who sits in a chair looking unwell. The owner reaches for a medicine bottle on a small table, warned by the dog's alert behaviour that sickness is coming.

pages.text: Search-and-Rescue Dogs Some dogs look for lost people. They are search-and-rescue dogs. Some smell the ground to find people.
pages.brief: A search-and-rescue dog moves through woodland with its nose pressed to the ground, following a scent trail, while its handler walks behind on a long lead. Fallen leaves and tree trunks fill the background of the search.

pages.text: Others smell the air. These dogs find lost hikers. They also find people under buildings that fall down.
pages.brief: Two search-and-rescue dogs work near a collapsed building, heads raised to sniff the air, rubble spread around them. In the distance a walking trail suggests lost hikers, the same dogs used to find people trapped under fallen structures.

pages.text: Some search-and-rescue dogs work in the water. They pull people to safety. These dogs need to swim well. Big, strong dogs make good water rescue dogs.
pages.brief: A big, strong dog swims in open water, pulling a person toward the shore, front legs driving through the waves. The dog's broad chest and steady stroke show the strength and swimming skill needed for water rescue work.

pages.text: Funny Jobs.
pages.brief: A simple section-opening picture with a light, playful mood. The page names only funny jobs, with no particular dog, place or action given, so keep the scene plain and uncluttered.

pages.text: Detection Dogs Some dogs use their nose to find hidden things. They are detection dogs. Police use these dogs to find criminals.
pages.brief: A detection dog sniffs along a row of low boxes and bags in an open yard, nose working carefully, a police handler standing close by. The dog's focused search shows hidden things being found by scent.

pages.text: These dogs smell buildings after a fire. They can smell chemicals. They can tell if someone started a fire on purpose.
pages.brief: After a fire, a detection dog sniffs the scorched wall and floor of a burnt building, handler beside it. Charred beams and ash are visible, showing the dog using its nose to pick out chemicals and tell how the fire began.

pages.text: Some insects eat wood. They ruin buildings by eating them. Detection dogs can find them before they eat too much.
pages.brief: A detection dog sniffs the wooden beams and boards of a building, nose close to small holes in the timber where insects have been eating the wood. The dog works before the damage spreads further through the structure.

pages.text: Conclusion Dogs do jobs to help us in many ways. They are smart and friendly. They have strong senses. They are some of the best workers around.
pages.brief: A gathering of working dogs with the people they help — a guide dog, a therapy dog and a search dog together in a bright outdoor space — smart, friendly animals with strong senses, shown as some of the best workers around.

books.title: Sharks
books.art_why: Sharks are real animals that exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Hundreds of kinds of sharks can be found all over the world Sharks have lived in the oceans since before Blue shark.
pages.brief: A blue shark glides through open blue ocean water, its slender body and pointed fins visible. Around it, other sharks of different shapes swim at a distance, suggesting many kinds of sharks found all over the world and living in oceans.

pages.text: Rays are close relatives of sharks Sharks are fish, but their skeletons are made instead of bones Cartilage is what gives human ears their shape Unlike most fish, sharks have rough skin.
pages.brief: A ray swims near a shark in clear ocean water, showing their close family link. The shark’s body is visible as a fish, and a human ear is shown separately to suggest flexible cartilage. The shark’s rough skin texture is shown close up.

pages.text: Sharks can sense other animals moving in the water They also see well in the dark Sharks have a good sense of smell Mako shark.
pages.brief: A mako shark swims through dark ocean water, its eye alert as it senses movement nearby. Small fish move in the dim water around it. Close views show its keen eye in the dark and its nose near drifting scent in the water.

pages.text: Sizes of sharks Sharks come in many sizes Some sharks are only a few inches long The huge whale shark is the largest fish in the world great white shark.
pages.brief: Sharks of very different sizes appear together in the ocean. A tiny shark only a few inches long swims near a huge whale shark, the largest fish in the world. A great white shark is shown nearby for comparison.

pages.text: This shading makes it harder for other animals to see them Many sharks are dark on the top and light on the bottom sneak up on other animals Shading helps sharks.
pages.brief: A shark swims in ocean water with a dark back and pale underside. Seen from below, its light belly blends with the bright surface, while from above its dark top blends with deep water. Other animals nearby remain unaware as the shark sneaks closer.

pages.text: Sharks swim by swinging their tails from side to side Fins help sharks, turn, and keep their balance.
pages.brief: A shark swims through the ocean, its tail swinging from side to side to push it forward. Its fins spread out as it turns and keeps its balance in the water. The shark’s body curves with the motion.

pages.text: When one tooth breaks off, another one moves up Most sharks have many rows of teeth thousand teeth during its lifetime. A shark may wear out and regrow a Do You Know? Lemon shark to take its place.
pages.brief: A lemon shark swims with its mouth partly open, showing many rows of teeth. One tooth is broken off, and another tooth moves up to take its place. Close views show replacement teeth ready in the rows behind.

pages.text: Do You Know? A great white shark can swallow a whole seal in one gulp. Great white shark Most sharks eat fish Large sharks eat sea lions, dolphins, and other sharks Some sharks eat shellfish These sharks have flat teeth for crushing shells.
pages.brief: A great white shark opens its mouth wide near a seal in the ocean, ready to swallow it in one gulp. Nearby, large sharks swim near sea lions and dolphins, while other sharks chase fish. One shark shows flat teeth for crushing shellfish.

pages.text: It swallows very small ocean plants and animals use them when eating The huge whale shark has tiny teeth but doesn’t   biggest fish alive today Whale sharks are the that float near the ocean’s.
pages.brief: A huge whale shark swims near the ocean’s surface with its mouth open, swallowing tiny ocean plants and animals floating in the water. Its tiny teeth are visible but not used for eating. It is the biggest fish alive today.

pages.text: Whitetip reef sharks are normally not dangerous to humans  Many people are afraid of sharks, but most sharks do not Great white sharks are one of the few kinds of sharks that are dangerous to people.
pages.brief: A whitetip reef shark swims in clear ocean water, looking calm and not threatening. A great white shark is shown nearby as one of the few kinds dangerous to people. A person at the water’s edge watches with fear, showing that many people are afraid of sharks.

pages.text: Many people eat shark meat, and shark fins are used to make soup People hunt sharks for their skin, oil, and teeth Shark fishing boats.
pages.brief: Shark fishing boats sit on the ocean with caught sharks on deck. People use shark meat for food, shark fins for soup, and shark skin, oil, and teeth. The scene shows the hunt and the different parts people take from sharks.

pages.text: Gray reef shark Many kinds of sharks are now in danger of being completely killed off Sharks are an important part of the balance of life in the world’s oceans They have as much right to live as any other animal.
pages.brief: A gray reef shark swims through a healthy ocean reef among other sea life. The scene shows sharks as an important part of the balance of life in the world’s oceans. Many kinds of sharks are in danger, and the image suggests they have a right to live.

pages.text: 12 (n.) surface to turn to move in a desired direction page 9 (v.) steer a group of reptiles that lived long ago page 4 (n.) dinosaurs an elastic tissue that makes up the skeletons of sharks, and rays page 5 (n.) cartilage.
pages.brief: The ocean surface meets the air above it, with waves rolling under the sky. A shark turns and steers through the water. Dinosaurs appear as reptiles from long ago, and a close view shows flexible cartilage in the skeletons of a shark and a ray.

books.title: Heroes of September 11
books.art_why: The book is about real people, dogs, buildings, and events from September 11, 2001, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Emergency New York City faced an emergency on September 11, 2001. Planes hit two huge buildings. The buildings caught fire. People inside needed to get out. Hurt people needed to find doctors. The fire left a mess that was not safe. Many brave heroes stepped in to help.
pages.brief: A wide view of New York City on September 11, 2001, with two huge buildings on fire after planes hit them. People inside hurry to get out, hurt people look for doctors, and brave helpers step in near the unsafe mess.

pages.text: Office Workers The burning buildings filled with smoke. It wasn’t safe to use the elevators. People rushed down the stairs.
pages.brief: Inside a burning building filled with smoke, office workers avoid the elevators and rush down the stairs. The crowded stairwell is smoky, and people hurry downward together to get out of the unsafe building.

pages.text: Two men saw a woman in a wheelchair on floor 68. They saw she needed help, so the men carried her to safety. Many office workers stopped to help others that day.
pages.brief: On floor 68 of a tall building, two men see a woman in a wheelchair who needs help. They carry her down toward safety. Around them, many office workers stop to help other people during the emergency.

pages.text: Dogs Not all the heroes were people. Some were dogs. About 400 dogs helped that day. Some dogs looked for hurt and lost people to rescue. Some dogs just helped people feel better.
pages.brief: About 400 dogs help during the emergency. Some dogs search for hurt and lost people to rescue. Other dogs stay close to people and help them feel better, showing that not all the heroes that day were people.

pages.text: One dog was inside when the fire started. She helped her owner, a blind office worker. The dog led her owner down to safety from floor 78!
pages.brief: Inside a building when the fire starts, a dog stays with her owner, a blind office worker. The dog leads her owner down from floor 78 to safety, guiding the way through the building.

pages.text: Firefighters Firefighters raced to the burning buildings and ran inside. They put themselves in danger to save others.
pages.brief: Firefighters race toward the burning buildings and run inside quickly without delay, wearing their heavy gear. They bravely put themselves in danger to save others, moving through smoke and heat in a serious emergency response.

pages.text: Other firefighters cleared the area around the burning buildings. They moved everyone away from danger.
pages.brief: Other firefighters work outside, calmly clearing the area around the burning buildings. They firmly move everyone away from danger, guiding people back and keeping the crowd at a safer distance while emergency work continues nearby.

pages.text: Firefighters looked for people to rescue. They found lost people and took hurt ones to doctors.
pages.brief: Firefighters search the buildings for people to rescue. They find lost people and lead them out, then take hurt people to doctors. Their careful search continues as they look for anyone still lost or hurt.

pages.text: Ironworkers The burned buildings fell down. Piles of broken walls and floors lay everywhere. These ruins were not safe.
pages.brief: The burned buildings have fallen down into huge piles. Broken walls and floors lie everywhere, forming unsafe ruins. The wreckage is dangerous, and the scene is blocked by debris where the tall buildings once stood.

pages.text: Ironworkers came from all over to help. Ironworkers are builders. Some of them had built the buildings that burned.
pages.brief: Ironworkers come from all over to help. These builders gather near the ruins, ready to work. Some of them had built the buildings that burned, and now they stand among the rubble to assist in the cleanup.

pages.text: The ironworkers had to work with care to clean up the ruins. They put themselves in danger every day until the mess was safe.
pages.brief: Ironworkers clean up the ruins slowly and with care, working among broken walls and floors each day. They put themselves in danger every day, using skill and caution until the unsafe mess is made safe again.

pages.text: Help in Hard Times This emergency showed how brave people and dogs can be. They faced danger to keep others safe. Sometimes they felt afraid, but fear didn‘t stop these heroes from helping others.
pages.brief: People and dogs who helped during the emergency stand together. They faced danger to keep others safe. Some look afraid but determined, showing that fear did not stop these heroes from helping others in hard times.

books.title: A Rainbow of Food
books.art_why: Real fruits and vegetables exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Did you know that you can eat a rainbow? You can’t eat a rainbow in the sky, of course. You can make a healthy rainbow out of all the different colors of fruits and vegetables.
pages.brief: A colorful arc made of different fruits and vegetables stretches across a plain background, showing red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple foods grouped like a healthy rainbow. No sky rainbow appears; the focus is the edible rainbow that people can make and eat.

pages.text: A red apple can help keep your heart strong. Eat some slices of this fruit for a healthy snack.
pages.brief: A shiny red apple sits whole beside several thin apple slices, all clearly red and fresh. The fruit is presented as a simple healthy snack, with the slices ready to eat and the whole apple showing its bright skin.

pages.text: Red raspberries can help keep you from getting sick. Eat a handful of this fruit instead of candy.
pages.brief: A small handful of bright red raspberries rests in a loose pile, with a few pieces of candy set nearby for contrast. The raspberries look fresh and juicy, showing the fruit as the snack chosen instead of candy.

pages.text: An orange carrot can help keep your eyes healthy. This vegetable is just plain fun to crunch between your teeth.
pages.brief: A bright orange carrot lies whole and crisp, with a cut piece nearby showing its crunchy texture. The vegetable is shown as a fun food to crunch, without any added person or setting beyond a clean, simple surface.

pages.text: An orange is filled with vitamins that can help keep you from catching a cold. Squeeze this fruit for some tangy juice with breakfast in the morning.
pages.brief: A whole orange sits beside a glass of tangy orange juice, with the fruit's bright peel and juicy inside visible. The juice is ready for breakfast, and the orange shows the vitamins and freshness described for a morning drink.

pages.text: A yellow banana can give you tons of energy. Peel and eat this fruit before you play.
pages.brief: A yellow banana is shown whole and peeled, with the soft fruit ready to eat. It sits in a simple setting as an energy-giving snack before play, with no person shown, only the bright banana and its peel.

pages.text: Yellow corn can help keep your stomach healthy. Munch this vegetable right off the cob at a picnic.
pages.brief: A yellow ear of corn on the cob is shown with bright kernels ready to munch. It rests in a picnic scene, with the corn as the clear focus and no people added, highlighting the vegetable as a crunchy snack.

pages.text: A green avocado can help your body take in all the stuff it needs. Squish up this fruit to make a creamy dip for chips.
pages.brief: A green avocado is shown cut open, with creamy green flesh ready to be squished. A bowl of creamy avocado dip sits beside it with a few chips, showing the fruit turned into a dip for chips.

pages.text: Green broccoli can help keep your bones strong. Pretend you are a dinosaur eating a tree and chow down on this vegetable.
pages.brief: A green broccoli floret stands tall like a small tree, with its thick stalk and branching top clearly visible. The vegetable is shown as a crunchy food to chow down, inviting a dinosaur-style pretend bite without adding any character.

pages.text: Blueberries can help you remember things. Eat this fruit every day to help you do well in school.
pages.brief: A pile of fresh blueberries is shown close up, with small round blue fruits clustered together. The berries look ready to eat as a daily fruit snack, with the focus on their bright color and the healthy boost for school.

pages.text: Purple plums help food move through your body. Get sticky with a bite of this juicy fruit.
pages.brief: A juicy purple plum is shown whole and cut open, with sticky, ripe flesh visible. The fruit looks ready for a bite, highlighting its juicy texture and the way it helps food move through the body.

pages.text: Purple grapes can help keep blood moving around your body. Toss a bunch of this fruit in the freezer and have a chilly treat.
pages.brief: A bunch of purple grapes is shown fresh and round, with some grapes placed in a freezer setting to become a chilly treat. The fruit is ready to toss in and freeze, focusing on the grapes and their purple color.

pages.text: These fruits and vegetables are just a few that can make up a food rainbow. Eating a rainbow every day is a fun and colorful way to stay healthy. How many colors will you eat today?
pages.brief: A colorful group of fruits and vegetables is arranged in a rainbow of colors, showing just a few foods that can make up a food rainbow. The bright spread invites a daily healthy choice, with many colors ready to eat.

books.title: Want to Be a Beaver?
books.art_why: The book includes extinct giant beavers and cutaway lodge views that a camera cannot capture.

pages.text: Want to Be a Beaver?
pages.brief: A beaver sits beside a quiet pond, looking toward the reader, with green plants and calm water around it. Soft sunlight falls on the scene, introducing the animal and its watery home. A few ripples spread across the pond.

pages.text: Beaver? Want to Be a.
pages.brief: A beaver swims through clear, shallow water near muddy banks and low green plants. Its broad flat tail trails behind it, and its small dark eyes stay above the surface as it moves forward. Ripples spread around its head.

pages.text: Do you like to play in water? Do you like to swim? If you do, then you might like life.
pages.brief: A beaver swims and splashes in a bright pond, rolling in the water with its tail kicking up spray. Green reeds line the bank, and the water looks cool and inviting, showing the playful side of life in a pond.

pages.text: When you’re a beaver, you can swim days after being born. As an adult, you can hold your breath for fifteen minutes.
pages.brief: An adult beaver glides underwater with a tiny young beaver beside it. The baby stays close, swimming just days after being born. The adult's sleek body moves through clear water, hinting at long breaths held beneath the surface.

pages.text: A set of clear eyelids allows you to see underwater. You can also close your nose and ears to keep out water. Do You Know? Beavers are not as big as they used to be. Long ago, beavers in North America were more than 8 feet (2.5 m) long–larger than a black bear today!
pages.brief: Underwater, a beaver floats with clear eyelids over its eyes and its nose and ears shut tight against the water. Nearby, an ancient giant beaver is shown beside a black bear, much larger than beavers today.

pages.text: Your four huge front teeth never stop growing! Chewing on wood all the time keeps them from growing too long. You can chew through a skinny tree in twenty minutes.
pages.brief: A beaver gnaws the trunk of a skinny tree beside a pond, its four huge front teeth pressed into the wood. Wood chips scatter on the ground, and the tree leans slightly as the beaver keeps chewing.

pages.text: Why do you want to chew through Dandy Dams In a week, a beaver family can build a dam that is 35 feet (10.7 m) long. Some dams, built over many years, have been more than 1,000 feet (305 m) long! Beaver dams create ponds, which provide a place to live for many plants as well as fish, turtles, frogs, birds, and other animals. Humans dislike the dams, though, when they flood human homes and farmland.
pages.brief: A beaver family works on a long dam of sticks and mud across a stream. Behind the dam, a pond spreads out with fish, turtles, frogs and birds nearby. In the distance, floodwater reaches human homes and farmland.

pages.text: Behind the dam, you build your A lodge is shaped like a dome and made of sticks and mud. In cold weather, the mud freezes hard. This keeps the lodge warm. Look Inside a Lodge underwater entrances.
pages.brief: A dome-shaped beaver lodge rises from a pond, built of sticks and mud. The frozen mud looks hard in cold weather. Below the water, dark entrances lead into the lodge, shown in a cutaway view.

pages.text: Your family, called a colony, lives in the lodge together. You and your mate stay together for many years.
pages.brief: Inside the lodge, a beaver family huddles together in a warm, dry space above the water. An adult pair stays close together while other beavers rest around them in the dim light of the lodge.

pages.text: As a beaver, you waste nothing. You eat the leaves, twigs, and bark of the trees you cut down. You store enough limbs under the water near your lodge to last all winter.
pages.brief: A beaver cuts down a tree and drags branches toward the water. Underwater near the lodge, a pile of limbs is stored for winter. On land, the beaver nibbles leaves, twigs and bark, wasting little of the tree.

pages.text: In the spring, you dine on ferns and water plants. You fill up on roots, too.
pages.brief: In spring, a beaver sits at the water's edge eating fresh ferns and water plants. Its paws hold roots and green stems, and new plants grow around the pond in the soft spring light. The pond is calm and bright.

pages.text: Storing food and working on your dam keeps you busy. You work mostly at night because you are nocturnal. Do You Know? When people work hard, we say they are “busy as a beaver.”
pages.brief: At night, a beaver works on its dam under moonlight, carrying sticks and patting mud into place. Its dark shape moves along the pond, busy storing food and repairing the dam while other animals sleep.

pages.text: Some animals hunt you because you’re slow on land. You’re safe in the water, though. When an enemy comes close, you slap the water with your flat, wide tail. The loud sound may warn other beavers.
pages.brief: A beaver stands on land, slow and exposed, while a hidden predator watches from nearby. Safe in the water, the beaver slaps its flat, wide tail on the surface, sending up a loud splash that warns other beavers.

pages.text: Your tail also helps you balance when you stand. It helps you steer when you swim. It even stores fat for the winter.
pages.brief: A beaver balances on its hind legs beside a stream, using its wide tail for support. In the water, the same tail steers as the beaver swims, and a cutaway shows fat stored inside for winter.

pages.text: If you like water and don’t mind work, then you might like being Beavers Live Here.
pages.brief: A beaver swims through a lively pond with plants, fish and other small animals around it. Near the water, a sturdy dam and lodge show where beavers live, inviting the reader to imagine life as a busy beaver.

books.title: Mexico
books.art_why: The keyword check points to drawing for illustrated maps and historical celebration scenes.

pages.text: Where Is It? Mexico is a country in North America. To the north of it is the United States. To the south of it is Central America. To the east and west of Mexico is the sea.
pages.brief: A wide illustrated view of Mexico in North America, with the United States lying to the north and Central America to the south. The sea stretches along the east and west sides of the country. The land and water fill the scene, showing Mexico’s place between its neighbors and the oceans.

pages.text: More than 120 million people live in Mexico. Most of them live in cities.
pages.brief: A crowded city street in Mexico, with many people walking, talking, and going about their day. Tall buildings and homes stand close together around them. More people fill the scene than in the countryside, showing that most of Mexico’s many millions of people live in cities.

pages.text: The capital of Mexico is Mexico City. It is one of the oldest cities in North America. It also has more people than any other city in North America!
pages.brief: Mexico City spreads out with old buildings beside busy modern streets. Crowds of people move through the capital, which is one of the oldest cities in North America. The city is packed with more people than any other city in North America, so the streets are full and lively.

pages.text: People Most people in Mexico speak Spanish. More people speak Spanish in Mexico than anywhere else.
pages.brief: Many people in Mexico speak Spanish together in a town square, at home, and in the street. More people speak Spanish in Mexico than anywhere else, so Spanish voices fill markets, schools, and neighborhoods. The scene shows a large group of people talking and listening in their everyday places.

pages.text: Land Mountains and canyons cover much of Mexico. Dry deserts are in the north. Forests cover land to the south. Two pieces of land stretch into the ocean. Baja (BAH-hah) is like a long finger. Yucatán (yoo-kah-TAHN) is more like a thumb.
pages.brief: Mountains and deep canyons cover much of Mexico. Dry desert stretches across the north, while forests cover land to the south. Two pieces of land reach into the ocean: one is long and fingerlike, and the other is rounded like a thumb. All these landforms appear together in a wide view.

pages.text: Animals Many different animals call Mexico home. Parrots, frogs, and many other animals live in the hot, wet forests. Foxes, lizards, and other animals live in the hot, dry deserts.
pages.brief: Parrots and frogs live among the hot, wet forests of Mexico, with leaves and branches around them. In the hot, dry deserts, foxes and lizards move across sandy ground. The picture shows these animals in their different homes, some in lush green forest and others in warm desert spaces.

pages.text: Celebrations People in Mexico celebrate many special days. The Day of the Dead lasts three days. It is a happy time. People remember their loved ones. They light candles and wear masks.
pages.brief: Families gather for the Day of the Dead, a happy three-day celebration. They remember loved ones together, light candles, and wear masks. Soft candlelight glows around them as they share memories in a warm, gentle scene. The people look calm and thoughtful, honoring those they love.

pages.text: People also remember the day long ago when Mexico began its fight to be free. They dress up and walk in parades. They light fireworks to celebrate.
pages.brief: People dress up in bright clothes and walk together in a parade. They remember the day long ago when Mexico began its fight to be free. Fireworks light up the sky above the marchers. The crowd celebrates with energy, moving through the streets in a festive, proud scene.

pages.text: Food Corn is an important food in Mexico. It is in almost every meal. People in Mexico also eat parts of cactus. They eat chicken and pork. Some people eat food from the sea.
pages.brief: Corn appears in almost every meal, shown in corn dishes and other food on a table. People also eat parts of cactus, chicken, pork, and food from the sea. A family meal brings these foods together, with dishes spread out and people ready to eat. The table looks full and colorful.

pages.text: People in Mexico often use peppers in their food. chile Some peppers are hot, like (CHIH-lee) peppers. Some peppers just make food taste different.
pages.brief: Peppers sit among food on a table, some small and hot, others just used to change the taste of a meal. People in Mexico often use peppers in their cooking. A person lifts a chile pepper near a plate, with more peppers nearby, showing how peppers add heat or flavor.

pages.text: Conclusion Mexico is an exciting country. Many different people and animals live there. What is your favorite thing about Mexico?
pages.brief: A lively view of Mexico brings together many different people and animals. Children and adults stand among parrots, frogs, foxes, and lizards, with mountains, forests, and city buildings in the background. The scene feels exciting and varied, inviting the viewer to think about a favorite thing in Mexico.

pages.text: Population: 127,575,529 Land: 1,964,375 sq km (758,450 sq. mi.) Capital City: Mexico City Primary Language: Spanish Currency: Peso (PAY-soh)
pages.brief: A busy Mexico City street shows the capital’s many people, with a crowd speaking Spanish and going about daily life. Coins sit nearby to suggest the country’s currency. Around the city, the wide land of Mexico stretches out. The scene gives a quick sense of the country’s people, capital, language, and money.

books.title: Brazil
books.art_why: The book describes present-day Brazil with real places, people, animals and cities that can be photographed.

pages.text: Brazil Where Is It? Brazil is the biggest country in South America. It covers almost half of the continent.
pages.brief: A wide aerial view of the South American continent, with Brazil’s large land area covering almost half of it. Green rainforest, tan plains, and mountain ranges spread across the continent, with ocean at the edges.

pages.text: Other countries border it to the north, south, and west. The Atlantic Ocean is to the east. The capital city of Brazil is Brasília (bruh-ZIL-yuh). Brasília became the capital in 1960. The city was built to be the capital. It was built in only a few years.
pages.brief: A modern capital city with wide avenues and bold government buildings spread across a flat landscape. The city looks newly built, with clean lines and open spaces. The Atlantic Ocean lies far to the east beyond the city.

pages.text: People More than two hundred million people live in Brazil. Most people in Brazil speak Portuguese (POR-chuh-geez).
pages.brief: A large crowd of many people of all ages stands together outdoors, children and adults talking to one another. The group is diverse and busy, suggesting more than two hundred million people living in Brazil.

pages.text: Most people in Brazil live in cities. Many of these cities are on coast the. Some people live in the country.
pages.brief: A coastal city with tall apartment buildings and houses along a sandy beach, the ocean waves nearby. In the distance, a small country home sits among green fields, showing that some people live outside the cities.

pages.text: Brazil Land Brazil has many different kinds of land. It has beaches and tall mountains. It also has flat land covered with water.
pages.brief: A wide landscape showing Brazil’s different kinds of land: a sandy beach by the sea in the foreground, tall rocky mountains rising behind, and flat wetland covered with shallow water stretching to one side. The scene is bright and open.

pages.text: Brazil is home to the Amazon rainforest. It covers almost half of Brazil. It is the biggest rainforest in the world. The Amazon River runs through the rainforest. It is one of the longest rivers in the world.
pages.brief: A dense green Amazon rainforest with tall trees and thick leaves. A wide river winds through the trees, reflecting the sky. The forest stretches far into the distance, covering almost half of the land. It is the biggest rainforest in the world.

pages.text: Celebrations People in Brazil celebrate Carnaval. The holiday happens during Brazil’s summer. It goes on for four days.
pages.brief: A sunny summer street filled with people celebrating Carnaval. Adults and children dance and move together under warm sunlight. The party fills the whole street during the four-day holiday. The celebration is lively and crowded.

pages.text: People dress up and walk in big parades. People play many different kinds of music. The party is one of the biggest in the world.
pages.brief: A big parade moving down a wide street. People dressed in elaborate, colorful costumes walk and dance in rows. Musicians play drums and other instruments, and a large crowd watches the biggest party in the world.

pages.text: Animals Many animals live in the Amazon rainforest. Parrots live there. They have colorful feathers. Colorful frogs live there, too. They live on the ground and in the trees.
pages.brief: A lush rainforest scene with bright parrots perched in tree branches, their colorful feathers spread. On the ground and on lower branches, colorful frogs sit among green leaves. The trees are tall and leafy. The rainforest is full of life.

pages.text: Many ants live in the rainforest. Fire ants and leaf-cutter ants live there. Many spiders live in the rainforest, too. The biggest spider in the world lives there.
pages.brief: The rainforest floor is busy with many ants. Leaf-cutter ants and fire ants crawl along the ground and up tree trunks. A very large spider rests on a low branch, the biggest spider in the world.

pages.text: Conclusion Brazil is an exciting country. It has big cities. It has forests filled with many animals. What do you like most about Brazil?
pages.brief: A wide view of Brazil showing a big city skyline on one side and a green forest full of animals on the other. Small animals move among the trees, and tall buildings rise in the distance. The country looks exciting and full of life.

pages.text: Population: 211,049,527 Land: 8,458,417 sq km (3,265,813 sq. mi.) Capital City: Brasília Primary Language: Portuguese Currency: Real (ray-AHL)
pages.brief: A collection of Brazilian real banknotes and coins resting on a wooden surface. Behind them, a modern view of Brasília’s buildings stands under a blue sky, and a large crowd of people fills a city street.

books.title: Egypt
books.art_why: Keyword check selects drawing, and the book includes ancient pharaohs, tombs, and pyramids that cannot be photographed as past events.

pages.text: Where Is It? Egypt is a country in North Africa. The Mediterranean (MEH-duh-tuh- RAY-nee-uhn) Sea is to the north. The Red Sea is to the east. Other countries are to the west and south.
pages.brief: A broad view of Egypt as a country in North Africa, shown together in one wide scene, with the Mediterranean Sea along its north side, the Red Sea to the east, and other countries to the west and south.

pages.text: The capital city of Egypt is Cairo (KEYE-roh). It is also one of the largest cities in Africa. More than twenty-one million people live there.
pages.brief: Cairo, the capital city of Egypt, shown in a wide city view as one of the largest cities in Africa, with more than twenty-one million people living there and many people moving through the busy city streets.

pages.text: People More than 106 million people live in Egypt. Most of them speak Arabic. Many people live in farming towns along the Nile River.
pages.brief: Many people in Egypt, more than 106 million, with most of them speaking Arabic, and many living in farming towns along the Nile River, shown together with families and workers in the towns and beside the river.

pages.text: Some farmers in Egypt grow cotton along the Nile. The cotton is used to make clothes. Farmers also grow rice, wheat, and other foods.
pages.brief: Farmers in Egypt growing cotton along the Nile in fields beside the river, with the cotton used to make clothes; nearby fields show rice, wheat, and other foods, with farmers working among the crops in the farming area.

pages.text: Land The desert stretches across all of Egypt. The Nile River runs through the east. It is the longest river in the world.
pages.brief: A wide view of Egypt with desert stretching across the land in one sweeping landscape and the Nile River running through the east, shown as the longest river in the world, flowing past desert ground.

pages.text: The Nile ends at the Mediterranean Sea. The land where the Nile ends is the Nile Delta.
pages.brief: The Nile River ending at the Mediterranean Sea, with the land where the river ends shown as the Nile Delta, spreading out along the coast in a wide view where river water meets the sea.

pages.text: Egypt also has mountains. Tall mountains rise in the east. Low mountains rise in the west.
pages.brief: Egypt with tall mountains rising in the east and low mountains rising in the west, shown in one wide landscape across the country, with the mountain slopes rising from the land seen at different heights.

pages.text: Animals Many animals live in Egypt. Foxes, lizards, and other animals live in the desert. Some people raise water buffalo, sheep, and goats. Some people use camels to travel from place to place.
pages.brief: Animals in Egypt, with a fox and a lizard in the desert; nearby people raise water buffalo, sheep, and goats, and a camel carries someone from place to place across the land in one scene.

pages.text: History Egypt is very old. Long ago, kings called pharaohs (FEHR-ohz) ruled the land. Some people believed the pharaohs were gods.
pages.brief: Long ago in Egypt, a king called a pharaoh rules the land as their ruler, with people around him believing the pharaoh is a god, shown in a very ancient grand scene before photographs existed.

pages.text: The pharaohs had huge pyramids (PIHR-uh-midz) built. These pyramids are tombs for the pharaohs. Gold treasures were placed in the tombs. Some of these treasures are in museums now.
pages.brief: Huge pyramids built for the pharaohs, shown as tombs, with gold treasures placed inside the tombs and some of those treasures now shown in museums, linking ancient tombs with museum displays clearly in one picture.

pages.text: Conclusion Egypt is an amazing country. It is also a very old country. Egypt has many important things to learn about.
pages.brief: A wide view of Egypt as a country, presented as an amazing and very old land with many important things to learn about; the scene focuses on the country itself and its long old history.

pages.text: Population: 106,156,692 Land: 995,450 sq km (622,272 sq. mi.) Capital City: Cairo Primary Language: Arabic Currency: Egyptian pound.
pages.brief: A wide view of Egypt showing its land and capital city Cairo, with Arabic-speaking people and Egyptian pound currency, presenting the country’s population, land area, capital, primary language, and currency together in one clear scene.

books.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
books.art_why: Real trees, leaves, and seasonal weather can be photographed.

pages.text: So Many Colors Why are the leaves on trees different colors? What makes them change color?
pages.brief: A group of trees stands outdoors under open daylight with leaves in many different colors, including green, yellow, orange, red, and brown. Some branches are full of one color, while other branches show several colors mixed together.

pages.text: Two Types of Trees.
pages.brief: Two different types of trees stand side by side in a natural outdoor setting. Each tree has its own shape and its own leaves, showing that trees can look different from one another, with branches spread wide.

pages.text: Making Food Leaves use sunlight, water, and air to make food for the tree. This way of making food is called photosynthesis. A chemical that helps leaves make food also makes them green.
pages.brief: A close-up shows green leaves on a tree branch in bright sunlight. Water droplets rest on the leaves, and air moves around the branch as the leaves make food for the tree. The leaves are full of green color.

pages.text: Photosynthesis is important to animals as well as plants. Some animals eat plants. Other animals eat those animals. Without photosynthesis, neither kind of animal would have food.
pages.brief: Outdoors, an animal eats leaves from a plant in a natural setting. Nearby, another animal that eats plant-eating animals stands alert. Both animals are connected to plants and to the food that green leaves make.

pages.text: Summer Summer is playtime. For the leaves of many trees, however, it’s work, work, work! The Sun is shining. The leaves are making food for the trees. The trees store any extra food deep inside. The stored food will help them get through winter.
pages.brief: In summer, the Sun shines brightly on a leafy tree. Green leaves work to make food for the tree, while extra food is stored deep inside the tree. The scene is warm and full of sunlight.

pages.text: Leaves are green in summer because they are making food. Leaves also have orange, yellow, or brown colors inside them. During summer, those other colors are hidden by the green color. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A close-up shows green summer leaves on a branch in bright daylight. Faint patches of orange, yellow, and brown lie hidden beneath the green color, waiting out of sight while the leaves make food for the tree.

pages.text: Fall Many places get colder in fall. The days get shorter, and the nights get longer. Trees get less sunlight, so photosynthesis slows down.
pages.brief: In fall, trees stand in a cooler landscape as the days grow shorter and the nights grow longer. Lower sunlight reaches the leaves, and the leaves' work of making food slows down. The sky looks dim.

pages.text: Over time, leaves stop making the green chemical, so they lose their green color. When that happens, the hidden orange, yellow, and brown colors start to show. Leaves also start making a red color at this time.
pages.brief: Close-up leaves on a branch in the fall air slowly lose their green color and begin to show orange, yellow, and brown. Some leaves also start to turn red as the green fades away from them.

pages.text: Once it gets cold enough to freeze at night, the trees drop their leaves. They do this to keep themselves safe. If the leaves freeze while still on the trees, the trees can be hurt.
pages.brief: On a cold night with frost on the ground, leaves fall from a tree and drift slowly down through the cold air. The tree is dropping its leaves away to keep itself safe from freezing.

pages.text: Winter Trees that drop their leaves are bare in winter. They use the stored food to get through the cold days and colder nights.
pages.brief: Bare trees stand in a winter scene with snow on the ground. Cold daylight fades toward an even colder night. The trees have dropped their leaves and rely on stored food to get through the cold.

pages.text: Spring Spring comes before long. Ice and snow melt, and the rains come. The Sun shines, and tiny leaves grow from branches.
pages.brief: Spring arrives with melting ice and snow, fresh rain falling, and the Sun shining. Tiny new leaves grow from the branches of trees. The wet ground and bright sky show the change from winter outdoors.

pages.text: Once again, the leaves use sunlight, water, and air to make food. The cycle begins again.
pages.brief: Fresh green leaves on a tree branch in bright daylight use sunlight, water, and air to make food for the tree once again. Water droplets and moving air surround the leaves as the cycle begins anew.

books.title: Ostriches: Giant Birds
books.art_why: Real ostriches, people, animals and African habitats can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: A Very Big Bird The ostrich is the biggest bird in the world. Most ostriches are taller than the tallest people.
pages.brief: A very large ostrich stands upright in an open outdoor setting beside two very tall people, making clear that the bird is taller than the tallest person. Its long neck, small head, feathers, and strong legs are visible as it towers over them.

pages.text: Ostriches have wings and feathers, but they can’t fly. An ostrich can run fast and far. It is the fastest animal with two legs. It runs faster than most four-legged animals.
pages.brief: An ostrich runs quickly across open ground, wings and feathers visible at its sides. Its long legs stretch out in a fast stride. In the distance, a four-legged animal is left behind, showing the ostrich is faster.

pages.text: Eyes on the Prize Ostriches have small heads with big eyes. Their eyes are bigger than those of any other land animal.
pages.brief: Close view of an ostrich’s small head and large eye, with its long neck and feathers visible. The eye is shown very big compared with the head, making clear that ostriches have very big eyes.

pages.text: Ostrich range AFRICA Ostrich Home, Sweet Home Most wild ostriches live in Africa. They live in small herds of ten or more birds.
pages.brief: Several wild ostriches stand together in a grassy African landscape, forming a small herd of ten or more birds. Their long necks and feathers are visible as they move among plants under an open sky.

pages.text: Ostriches use teamwork to stay safe. Their sharp eyes and long necks help them spot danger from far away.
pages.brief: A group of ostriches stands alert in open grassland, their long necks raised high as they look out for danger. Their sharp eyes scan the distance while the herd stays close together, using teamwork to stay safe.

pages.text: What’s on the Menu? Ostriches eat grass, other plants, and fruit. They also eat bugs and other small animals. Ostriches don’t drink much water. They get water from the plants and fruit they eat.
pages.brief: An ostrich pecks at grass, leafy plants, fruit, and small bugs on the ground. It stands in an open outdoor area with plants around it, eating the foods it needs and getting water from what it eats.

pages.text: Look Out! Run! Lions and cheetahs hunt ostriches for food. Ostriches must be on the lookout. Their long necks help them look far. They have strong legs and big feet. An ostrich can kick very hard. Its kick can kill a lion.
pages.brief: A lion approaches an ostrich in open grassland. The ostrich stands ready on strong legs with big feet, looking toward the lion. Its long neck helps it watch from far away as it prepares to kick hard.

pages.text: Ostriches make a loud noise when they see a lion. The noise warns other animals that lions are near.
pages.brief: An ostrich stands with its beak wide open, making a loud call. Nearby animals hear the noise in the open landscape, warned that a lion is near. The ostrich’s long neck and feathers are visible.

pages.text: From Big Egg to Big Bird A male ostrich digs a shallow pit in the dirt for a nest. The mother lays her eggs in the pit. In six weeks, baby ostriches hatch from the eggs. A baby ostrich is the size of a grown chicken.
pages.brief: A male ostrich digs a shallow pit in the dirt for a nest. A female ostrich stands near the pit where her eggs lie. The scene shows the nest on open ground, with the parent birds close to their eggs.

pages.text: An ostrich chick grows about 1 foot (30 cm) per month. In six months, the baby ostrich will be grown. It can live for fifty years or more.
pages.brief: An ostrich chick stands beside a grown ostrich in an open outdoor area. The chick is growing bigger month by month, and the adult shows how large it will become. Both birds have feathers and long legs.

pages.text: Conclusion Ostriches are special birds. They are strong and fast. Ostriches are bigger than any other bird.
pages.brief: A large, strong ostrich stands or runs in an open outdoor setting, its long neck and feathers clear. Its size shows it is bigger than other birds. Its strong legs show it is fast and powerful.

books.title: Goliath Beetles: Giant Insects
books.art_why: Goliath beetles, African forests and zoos all exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: The World’s Biggest Beetle Goliath beetles are the giants of the insect world. Adult Goliaths can be bigger than a songbird. A young Goliath beetle is called a larva. A larva can be even bigger than an adult beetle!
pages.brief: A large adult Goliath beetle with a striped shell stands on a tree branch beside a small songbird, showing the beetle is bigger. Below on the forest floor lies a huge white larva, larger still than the adult beetle, curled among leaves.

pages.text: What Is a Beetle? All beetles have two sets of wings. The large wings in the back are for flying. The front wings are smaller and harder. They protect the flying wings.
pages.brief: A Goliath beetle on a branch with its hard front wings lifted open, showing the large thin back wings spread for flying. The smaller, tougher front wings are held out to the sides, lifted away from the flying wings.

pages.text: Beetles have mouths that help them chew. Some insects, like butterflies, have mouths like straws. Other insects have mouths like needles.
pages.brief: Close view of a Goliath beetle's chewing mouth as it bites into a piece of fruit on the forest floor. Nearby, a butterfly sips with its long straw-like mouth, and another insect with a thin needle-like mouth rests on a leaf.

pages.text: Little Zebras Most Goliath beetles have black stripes. Some beetles are plain brown. No two beetles are the same. People once called Goliath beetles “zebra beetles” because of their stripes.
pages.brief: Two Goliath beetles on a tree trunk in an African forest, one with bold black stripes on its shell and another plain brown. Their stripe patterns differ, no two markings alike, as they cling to the bark in the shade.

pages.text: An African Home Goliath beetles live in forests and grassy parts of Africa.
pages.brief: Goliath beetles moving through an African landscape where dense green forest meets open grassy ground. Several beetles walk among the grasses and low plants, some climbing on fallen wood under warm sunlight, in the places where they live.

pages.text: They are only seen during the rainy time of year. That’s when there is plenty of fruit for them to eat. Male Goliath beetles fight other males over feeding places. Male beetles may get mates by having good feeding places.
pages.brief: During the rainy season, two male Goliath beetles lock horns and push each other over a pile of ripe fruit on the wet forest floor, while a female beetle watches nearby. Rain falls through the leaves and drips onto the ground.

pages.text: Big Changes Female Goliath beetles put their eggs in a deep hole. Larvae hatch about two weeks later. The larvae eat dead plants in the soil and grow fast.
pages.brief: A female Goliath beetle digs into soft soil and lays eggs in a deep hole. Beside her, tiny larvae have hatched and are eating bits of dead plants in the dark earth, their small bodies curled as they feed and grow.

pages.text: Larvae can be as long as your hand. They are as heavy as five mice! As soon as the rain ends, the larvae go deep into the ground. They cover themselves with a thin coat of sand.
pages.brief: A large white larva lies stretched beside a child's open hand to show its length, thick and heavy. Deeper in the soil, larvae crawl down and cover themselves with a thin coat of sand as the rain stops above.

pages.text: Larvae change into adult beetles inside the coat of sand. Adults come out when the rain begins again.
pages.brief: Inside a thin sand-coated shell in the ground, a larva changes into an adult beetle. Above, rain begins to fall on the forest floor, and a new adult Goliath beetle pushes out of the sandy coat and climbs onto the wet ground.

pages.text: A Short Life In zoos, Goliath beetles live to be about eight months old. In the wild, Goliath beetles must find food and escape enemies. They may only live for a few months.
pages.brief: A Goliath beetle inside a zoo enclosure rests on a log near leaves and fruit. In the wild, another beetle hurries across the forest floor to find food, hiding from a watching bird and other enemies among the plants and shadows.

pages.text: Conclusion People have been studying Goliath beetles for hundreds of years. They are rare and interesting to see. Goliath beetles are amazing insects!
pages.brief: Scientists crouch low in an African forest, watching and studying a striped Goliath beetle on a branch, notebooks in hand. The rare beetle stays still on the bark while the people observe it closely in the dappled light.

books.title: Goliath Bird-Eating Spiders: Giant Arachnids
books.art_why: Goliath bird-eating spiders are real animals that exist today.

pages.text: A Big, Hairy Spider Goliath bird-eating spiders are very big spiders. They are about the size of a dinner plate. They weigh more than any other spider in the world.
pages.brief: A very large, hairy Goliath bird-eating spider stands on the dark rainforest floor. Its body is thick and covered with hairs, and it looks as wide as a dinner plate. It is shown alone, heavy and big, weighing more than any other spider in the world.

pages.text: Like many spiders, Goliath spiders have eight legs and eight eyes. Even with that many eyes, they can’t see very well. Their bodies are covered with many tiny hairs.
pages.brief: A close-up of a Goliath spider shows its eight legs and eight eyes. The spider rests on the forest ground, its body covered with many tiny hairs. Its eyes are small, and it does not look sharp-eyed as it stays still.

pages.text: Two Body Parts Spiders have two body parts. The mouth, fangs, and legs are in the front part. The back part is for making silk.
pages.brief: A Goliath spider is shown from the side so its two body parts are clear. The front part holds its mouth, fangs, and legs. The back part makes silk, and a thin silk thread comes from it as the spider stands on the rainforest floor.

pages.text: A spider with its legs can be about 1 foot (30 cm) across. That’s as long as a ruler!
pages.brief: A Goliath spider stretches its legs wide across the ground. Its legs reach out far from its body, showing a span about one foot across. The spider is alone on the forest floor, its long legs spread as wide as a ruler.

pages.text: Home in the Rainforest Goliath spiders live in rainforests. The forests are in hot and wet parts of the world. The spiders make their homes burrows in under the ground.
pages.brief: A Goliath spider sits at the entrance of a burrow under the ground in a hot, wet rainforest. Green plants and damp soil surround it. The spider's home is a hole in the earth, and it stays close to the opening in the warm, wet forest.

pages.text: What’s for Dinner? Goliath spiders are great hunters. They hunt at night for mice, insects, and other small prey. The hairs on their body help them sense when a small animal is near.
pages.brief: At night in the rainforest, a Goliath spider hunts near a small mouse and insects. The spider's body hairs help it sense the small animal nearby. The dark forest floor is dim, and the spider is close to its prey, ready to hunt.

pages.text: When Goliath spiders hunt, they get close to a small animal. Then they grab it with their strong, hairy legs.
pages.brief: A Goliath spider gets close to a small animal on the rainforest floor. Then it grabs the animal with its strong, hairy legs. The spider holds on tightly, its legs wrapped around the prey as it catches it in the dark forest.

pages.text: Poison Fangs Giant Goliath spiders have a special weapon. Their fangs are filled with poison. When they bite an animal, the poison makes the animal stop moving. Humans don’t need to worry too much. A bite from a Goliath spider hurts about as much as a wasp sting.
pages.brief: A close-up shows a Goliath spider's fangs, filled with poison. The spider is near a small animal it has bitten, and the animal has stopped moving. The fangs are sharp and ready, showing the spider's special weapon in the rainforest.

pages.text: Watch Out for Enemies Even big spiders have enemies. Hawks, owls, and snakes sometimes eat Goliath spiders. An insect called a spider wasp can kill them, too.
pages.brief: A Goliath spider stands on the forest floor while enemies are nearby. A hawk and an owl are shown above, a snake moves close, and a spider wasp hovers near the big spider. These animals sometimes eat or kill Goliath spiders in the rainforest.

pages.text: Growing Up Baby spiders hatch from eggs. They look like little adults. They must shed their outside skin to grow bigger. They shed their skin many times during their lives.
pages.brief: Baby Goliath spiders hatch from eggs and look like tiny adults. One small spider is shedding its outside skin so it can grow bigger. The young spiders are on the rainforest floor, and the shed skin lies nearby as they grow.

pages.text: Learning from Spiders Huge, hairy Goliath spiders are very special. They have an important job in their forest homes. We can learn a lot from them!
pages.brief: A huge, hairy Goliath spider stands in its rainforest home. It is shown as a special spider with an important job in the forest. The big spider rests among damp plants and soil in its forest home.

books.title: Incredible Places to Stay
books.art_why: All the hotels are real places that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: 2 6 3 7 4 Introduction Do you want to see some of the world’s most amazing hotels? Let’s go!
pages.brief: A bright opening view of several extraordinary hotels in far-off landscapes, one high on a mountainside, one built of ice, one among tall trees, inviting the reader to set off and see the world's most amazing places to stay.

pages.text: Sky High Your tour starts in the Sacred Valley of Cuzco, Peru. At Skylodge Adventure Suites, you can sleep high in the air.
pages.brief: The Sacred Valley of Cuzco, Peru, with green mountains rising steeply. High above the valley floor, a small suite hangs in the air on the cliff face, where a guest can sleep far above the ground.

pages.text: A Cool Place to Stay The next stop is the Hôtel de Glace (O-tel DEH GLAHS) in Canada. Many parts of the hotel are made of ice.
pages.brief: The Hôtel de Glace in Canada, its walls, doorway and furniture carved from ice, glowing pale blue in cold winter light, with snow on the ground around the icy building.

pages.text: The ice melts away in the spring. Workers build the hotel again each winter.
pages.brief: The same ice hotel in spring, its walls melting and dripping away, while workers in warm clothes lift fresh blocks of ice and rebuild the hotel again for the next winter.

pages.text: Breakfast with Giraffes From Canada, you’ll travel to Kenya. Giraffes live in the forests around a hotel called Giraffe Manor. Giraffes come to the hotel every morning to eat.
pages.brief: Giraffe Manor in Kenya, a low building surrounded by green forest. Tall giraffes wander between the trees and stride up to the hotel in the morning, stretching their long necks toward it to eat.

pages.text: If you stay there, you can feed them!
pages.brief: Close beside the Kenyan hotel, a tall giraffe lowers its head to a guest who holds out food, the giraffe's patterned neck curving down and its face close to the person's hands.

pages.text: In the Trees The next stop on your tour is Sweden. The Treehotel is made up of many tree houses. The Mirrorcube has glass all around it. This tree house blends in with the woods.
pages.brief: The Treehotel in Sweden, a group of tree houses held among tall trunks. The Mirrorcube is covered in glass on every side, its mirrored walls reflecting the surrounding woods so it blends into the forest.

pages.text: One tree house looks like a big bird’s nest. The UFO tree house looks like a spaceship from outer space.
pages.brief: Two unusual tree houses among the Swedish trees: one shaped like a huge bird's nest of woven branches, the other shaped like a spaceship from outer space, standing on a trunk in the woods.

pages.text: A Room Without a View You also stop at the Sala Silvermine Hotel in Sweden. It has the deepest hotel room in the world! It is a long way down to your room. Dress in warm clothes! The mine is cold.
pages.brief: The Sala Silvermine Hotel in Sweden, a dark rocky mine shaft going deep underground. A long drop leads down to the deep hotel room, and a guest dressed in warm clothes stands in the cold tunnel.

pages.text: Sleeping with Fish Your last stop is Jules’ Undersea Lodge in Florida. You have to swim down to reach your room!
pages.brief: Jules' Undersea Lodge in Florida, sitting underwater. A guest in swimwear dives down through blue water toward the lodge, swimming to reach the room below the surface.

pages.text: You can even order a pizza from your room. Someone from the hotel will swim it down to you.
pages.brief: Inside the underwater room in Florida, a pizza box waits while a hotel worker in diving gear swims down through the water outside, carrying the pizza to the guest's room.

pages.text: Conclusion It is time to go back home now. All of these hotels are more than just places to stay. Each one is incredible! Polar Bear Fun.
pages.brief: A last look back at the journey home, with the travellers' route ending and the memory of the cliff suite, the ice hotel, the giraffe hotel, the tree houses, the mine and the undersea lodge — each one incredible.

books.title: Cricket
books.art_why: The book includes cricket's history from the 1500s, before photographs existed, so drawings fit.

pages.text: A Fun Sport People around the world play an exciting sport called cricket. In cricket, a batter hits a ball with a large flat bat. The ball is about the same size as a baseball.
pages.brief: A cricket batter swings a large flat bat at a small ball on an oval field, while nearby players watch. The ball is about the same size as a baseball. The scene suggests people around the world enjoying this exciting sport.

pages.text: The Basics Two teams play a game of cricket. Each team has eleven players. They play on an oval field with an area in the middle. The field is called a pitch.
pages.brief: Two cricket teams of eleven players each stand on an oval field, ready to play. In the middle is an area called the pitch. Players are positioned around the field, with the pitch in the center.

pages.text: The teams take turns batting and bowling, or throwing, a ball. Two batters on the batting team stand on each end of the pitch. The team that isn’t batting plays in the field.
pages.brief: Two batters from one team stand at opposite ends of the pitch, each holding a bat. A player from the other team bowls the ball toward them. The rest of the bowling team spreads out in the field, waiting to field.

pages.text: One player on each team is the bowler. The bowler throws a ball to a batter on the other team.
pages.brief: A bowler from one team stands on the pitch and throws a cricket ball toward a batter from the other team. The batter waits with a bat, ready to hit the ball during the game.

pages.text: The bowler tries to hit three small posts in the ground near the batter. These posts are called stumps. At the top of the stumps are two small pieces of wood called bails. Together, the stumps and bails are called a wicket. If the bowler’s ball knocks the bails off the wicket stumps, the batter is out.
pages.brief: A bowler sends the ball toward three small posts set in the ground near the batter. Two small pieces of wood rest on top of the posts; together they form the wicket. The ball knocks the top pieces off, and the batter is out.

pages.text: The batter protects the wicket by hitting the ball with his or her bat. If the batter hits the ball, he or she runs down the pitch. If the batter swaps places with the other batter, he or she scores one point. The point is called a run.
pages.brief: A batter hits the ball with a bat to protect the wicket, then runs down the pitch. The other batter runs toward the opposite end. As the two batters swap places, the batting team scores one run.

pages.text: Nine players on the bowling team play in the field. Their job is to get the balls that the batter hits. They can get the batter out by catching the ball. They can also throw the ball and hit the wicket to get an out. After ten outs, the bowling team gets their turn at bat. At the end of the game, the team with more runs wins.
pages.brief: Nine fielders from the bowling team stand in the field, watching the batter. One fielder catches the ball to get an out; another throws the ball at the wicket. The fielders work to end the batting turn.

pages.text: The History of Cricket In the 1500s, children in England played cricket. By the early 1700s, adults started playing as professionals. In 1788, people created the cricket rules still in use today.
pages.brief: In an old English setting, children play an early form of cricket with a bat and ball. Nearby, adults play as professionals. A group of people writes down cricket rules that are still used today.

pages.text: Soon, cricket teams formed outside England as well. Then, people created longer cricket matches called Tests for world championships.
pages.brief: Cricket teams from countries outside England form and gather on an oval field to play. Players take part in a longer match called a Test, competing for a world championship. The field is busy with players from different teams.

pages.text: Cricket teams played once at the Olympic Games in 1900. Some fans hope cricket teams will one day play in every Summer Olympic Games.
pages.brief: A cricket team plays a match at the Olympic Games in 1900. Players stand on the field with bats and a ball. Fans watch from the side and hope cricket will one day be part of every Summer Olympic Games.

pages.text: Cricket Around the World Today, people play cricket around the world. Twelve countries have teams that play in Test matches.
pages.brief: People play cricket around the world today. Players from many countries stand on an oval field with bats, a ball, and a wicket, taking part in a match. Twelve national teams have teams that play in Test matches.

pages.text: That’s Cricket! Since its start as a children’s game, cricket has been popular. Today, it is followed by billions of fans around the world. You can enjoy cricket, too!
pages.brief: A lively cricket match is in progress, with batters, bowlers, and fielders on the oval field. Since its start as a children's game, cricket has remained popular. A crowd of fans watches the game, and the scene invites readers to enjoy cricket, too.

pages.text: A line connects two points. A line is longer than it is wide. Lines can be short, and lines can be long. Lines can be straight, and lines can be curved.

pages.brief: A flat surface displays a circle, a square, a rectangle, and a triangle spaced apart. Around them, simple drawings made from those same geometric shapes appear, showing how the shapes can be combined to draw objects. The shapes are clear and separate.

pages.brief: A piece of paper shows a drawn rectangle. It has been turned into a house by adding a roof, two windows, and a door. A triangle and three rectangles are used for these parts. The rectangle forms the house’s main body, and the completed house sits alone on the paper.
