books.title: Argentina
books.art_why: This is a modern country profile - real cities, people, animals, mountains and food that can all be photographed today.

pages.text: Where Is It? Argentina is the second-largest country in South America. It is the eighth-largest country in the world. Five countries share borders with Argentina.
pages.brief: A wide view of the southern half of South America, with Argentina filling most of the land from the mountains in the west to the ocean in the east. Long borders touch five neighbouring countries, and broad plains stretch across the middle.

pages.text: About forty-three million people live in Argentina. capital The of Argentina is Buenos Aires. Its name means “fair winds.” About fifteen million people live there.
pages.brief: A busy street in Buenos Aires, Argentina's capital, with tall buildings, buses and crowds of people walking under a windy sky. Green parks and open squares sit between the buildings where around fifteen million people live.

pages.text: People Most people in Argentina live in big cities. Other people live in the country. Some of these people are farmers. They grow crops such as wheat and grapes.
pages.brief: Farmers working in the countryside outside the big cities, cutting golden wheat and picking bunches of grapes in a vineyard. Farmhouses and open fields stretch behind them as crates of grapes are loaded onto a truck.

pages.text: People from all over the world live in Argentina. Europe Many are from. Most people in Argentina speak Spanish.
pages.brief: A crowded city pavement where families from many parts of the world walk together, including people whose families came from Europe. Friends stop to chat in Spanish outside a cafe, smiling, with shop fronts behind them.

pages.text: Land Argentina has mountains, lakes, and rivers. The Andes Mountains are in the west. They are the longest group of mountains in the world.
pages.brief: The Andes Mountains rising in the west, long snowy ridges stretching away to the horizon. Below them lie a blue lake and rivers winding through valleys, with small trees along the shore under a clear sky.

pages.text: Argentina has many kinds of animals. Monkeys, wild cats, and many other animals live there. Argentina has some lovely rivers. Some of the river water falls from very high places. The falls are some of the biggest in the world.
pages.brief: A monkey swinging through a leafy branch and a wild cat padding along a forest path. Nearby, a huge waterfall crashes down a cliff with mist rising, and the river runs on through green jungle.

pages.text: History People have lived in Argentina for thousands of years. Long ago, the Spanish ruled the country. Then, army leaders took control.
pages.brief: An old colonial square with Spanish-style stone buildings and a church, people in long-ago dress walking past. Beyond the town, open grassland where native people lived for thousands of years before Spanish rule.

pages.text: The army leaders did not let people have any say in their rules. This was unfair for most people. Today, people in Argentina can help make rules. They choose leaders who share their ways of thinking.
pages.brief: People of all ages standing in line at a polling station, holding papers and placing votes in a box. Families talk together outside the building, choosing the leaders they want, with a flag above the door.

pages.text: Celebration One of the biggest parties in Argentina lasts for days. People dress up as clowns and animals. They have a lot of fun. There is music and dancing. There is a big parade.
pages.brief: A street parade with dancers in bright costumes dressed as clowns and animals, wearing masks and painted faces. Drummers play and crowds cheer along the road while confetti falls and children dance beside the dancers.

pages.text: Food People in Argentina eat meat cooked on a grill. They also eat little pies filled with meat, vegetables, or cheese.
pages.brief: A family barbecue in a garden, slabs of meat sizzling on a grill over glowing coals. On a table nearby sit little golden pies filled with meat, vegetables and cheese, and people reach for them, laughing.

pages.text: Conclusion Argentina is a country with people from all over the world. They help to make it a great place with a bright tomorrow.
pages.brief: A group of Argentinian people of many ages and backgrounds standing together in a city park, children, grandparents and workers smiling at each other, with tall buildings and leafy trees behind them in the sunlight.

pages.text: Population: 43,646,358 Land: 2,736,690 sq km (1,056,642 sq. mi.) Capital City: Buenos Aires Primary Language: Spanish Primary Religion: Roman Catholic Name of Currency: Argentine peso.
pages.brief: A wide view of Buenos Aires on a sunny day: busy streets, a large cathedral and government buildings, people walking and talking in Spanish, and a corner bank with pigeons on the pavement outside.

books.title: Sled Dogs to the Rescue
books.art_why: A 1925 Alaska medicine relay is a historical event best shown in drawn scenes, as the brief's keyword check suggests.

pages.text: A Terrible Disease In January 1925, a big storm The Great Sled Dog Relay hit Alaska. The medicine was passed from The medicine came by train team to team. Two Native children in a town in and was given to the first team. It often had to be warmed Alaska died. Others were very sick The race was on. by the fire. and needed medicine.
pages.brief: A small Alaska town in January 1925, buried in a big storm. Inside a wooden house, two Native children lie sick in bed under blankets. A train has arrived with the medicine, and a sled dog team takes the package. Near a fire, the medicine is warmed before it goes on.

pages.text: The medicine could be brought part of the way by train. There were still 674 miles (1,085 km) to the town.
pages.brief: A steam train pushes through deep snow and stops at the end of the line. A sled dog team waits beside the tracks with an empty sled, ready for the medicine. Beyond them a long white trail runs away toward a far-off town, still 674 miles distant.

pages.text: Sled dog teams had to bring it the rest of the way.
pages.brief: Sled dog teams run in a line along a snowy trail, each one taking the medicine from the team ahead. Dogs lean into their harnesses, breath steaming, paws kicking up snow as the relay carries the package on through the winter wilderness.

pages.text: One driver and his lead dog, Togo, raced for more miles than any other team.
pages.brief: One driver stands on the runners of his sled behind a hard-working dog team, his lead dog Togo out front. Togo pulls ahead through the snow, ears up, running the longest stretch of the whole relay while the driver guides the sled behind him.

pages.text: The Dogs Deliver Another driver and his lead dog, Balto, raced in a blizzard.
pages.brief: A second driver rides his sled behind another lead dog, Balto, as a blizzard howls around them. Snow blows sideways, the dogs' heads are low, and the driver leans forward, keeping the medicine safe as the team pushes on through the storm.

pages.text: At one point, the wind blew them over. The driver had to dig the medicine out of the snow.
pages.brief: The wind knocks the sled over in the deep snow. The driver kneels and digs with his hands, searching for the medicine where it fell. Beside him the dogs stand half-buried, waiting, while snow swirls past and the blizzard keeps blowing.

pages.text: When the last team was not ready to leave, Balto’s team went on instead. Five and a half days after the race began, they made it to the town.
pages.brief: Balto's team sets off when the last team is not ready, running the final stretch alone. They arrive in the town five and a half days after the race began, dogs tired and coats frozen, people coming out into the snow to meet them.

pages.text: After the Race After the race, Togo’s team went all over the United States. Balto’s team did, too.
pages.brief: After the race, Togo's team and Balto's team travel all over the United States. The dogs walk through city streets with crowds of people around them, standing beside their drivers far from the Alaskan snow.

pages.text: Balto’s team lived the rest of their lives in a zoo. famous Balto was the most of the sled dogs.
pages.brief: Balto's team lives the rest of their lives in a zoo enclosure. Balto stands apart, the most famous of the sled dogs, while visitors lean on the fence to look at him. The other dogs rest nearby on the ground behind him.

pages.text: However, the other dogs also helped save the sick children when there was little hope.
pages.brief: The other sled dogs stand together in the snow outside the town, the whole team that carried the medicine. In a warm window nearby, the children who were sick are sitting up again, saved when there was very little hope.

books.title: Amazing Antarctica
books.art_why: Antarctica, its animals, scientists and visitors are real and can be photographed.

pages.text: North America Africa Antarctica South America Asia Europe Australia The Seventh Continent Give a globe a spin. You can easily find six continents. Now look at the bottom of the globe. You will find continent number seven. It’s Antarctica!
pages.brief: A globe fills the view, turned to show six continents across its surface. Antarctica sits at the very bottom of the globe, set apart from the others. The southern continent is clearly visible as continent number seven.

pages.text: People found Antarctica about two hundred years ago. We have learned a lot about this amazing place.
pages.brief: People step onto Antarctica’s icy land for the first time, with a wide white landscape around them. The scene looks back to about two hundred years ago, when people found the continent. It suggests the amazing place they would learn much about.

pages.text: Antarctica is the coldest continent. It also has the strongest winds. Less rain and snow fall there than in other places.
pages.brief: Antarctica appears as a huge frozen continent under a pale sky. Strong wind sweeps loose snow across the ice, showing the continent’s powerful winds. The air looks bitterly cold. Only a little snow falls in the distance, matching the small amount of rain and snow that reaches this place.

pages.text: Freezing Antarctica Water covers most of Earth. Almost all of it is salt water. Most of the fresh water is frozen in Antarctica’s ice. Snow does not melt during the summers. The ice builds up over many years.
pages.brief: Most of Earth is covered by water, and almost all of that water is salt water. In Antarctica, thick ice holds most of the world’s fresh water. Snow piles up and does not melt during the summers, so the ice builds higher over many years.

pages.text: Life on and Around Antarctica Freezing weather makes Antarctica a dangerous place to live.
pages.brief: Freezing weather covers Antarctica’s icy ground. The cold, harsh conditions make the continent a dangerous place for living things. Snow and ice stretch across the scene, while the empty, frozen landscape shows how hard it is to survive in such a severe environment.

pages.text: Most plants and animals live near or in the sea. There are no trees. There are other plants, such as moss.
pages.brief: Most plants and animals in Antarctica live near or in the sea. On the icy land, there are no trees. Small plants such as moss cling to the cold ground. The scene shows the sea nearby and the low plant life that manages to grow in this harsh place.

pages.text: Penguins and seals are some of the larger animals in Antarctica. Wowser!
pages.brief: Penguins and seals are some of the larger animals in Antarctica. Penguins stand together on the ice near the water, while seals rest on the frozen ground nearby. The animals are shown in the cold Antarctic setting, surrounded by ice and sea.

pages.text: A Playground for Scientists People made sure that scientists can study in Antarctica. Do You Know?
pages.brief: Scientists stand together in Antarctica’s snowy landscape, ready to study the frozen continent. Open ice and sky stretch around them, showing the place people made sure scientists could use for research. The scene focuses on the scientists and the cold, wide environment that surrounds their work.

pages.text: Many countries send scientists to study in Antarctica. Some work there all year. Others work only in summer.
pages.brief: Many countries send scientists to study in Antarctica. Some scientists work there all year, while others work only in summer. In the scene, scientists are busy in the cold landscape, with the wide ice and sky showing the remote place where they carry out their studies.

pages.text: Many kinds of scientists come to Antarctica. They study animals and ice. They study many other things.
pages.brief: Many kinds of scientists come to Antarctica. They study animals and ice, and they study many other things. In the scene, scientists observe animals nearby and examine the thick ice around them. The frozen landscape shows the wide range of subjects that bring researchers to the continent.

pages.text: Thousands of visitors also come to Antarctica each year.
pages.brief: Thousands of visitors come to Antarctica each year. In the scene, many visitors stand on the icy ground, looking across the cold landscape. More people are scattered in the distance, showing the large number of visitors who travel to this remote place. Ice and sky stretch around them.

pages.text: Conclusion People do not know a lot about Antarctica. The cold, wind, and rough seas make it a hard place to visit. However, people do know it is important to protect Antarctica.
pages.brief: Antarctica is shown as a cold, windy continent with rough seas around its edges. The harsh conditions make it a hard place to visit, and much about it remains unknown. Even so, the scene suggests that people know it is important to protect this frozen land.

books.title: The Amazing Octopus
books.art_why: Octopuses are real animals that live in the ocean today.

pages.text: Introduction More than three hundred types of octopuses live in ocean waters around the world. Their interesting looks and incredible skills make octopuses amazing creatures of the sea.
pages.brief: A wide ocean scene shows several different octopuses in blue water around the world. One large octopus spreads its eight arms near rocks, while smaller octopuses hover above the seafloor. Their big eyes, soft bodies and long arms are clearly visible as they float together.

pages.text: How Are Octopuses Born? Mother octopuses watch over their hatch eggs until they. It could take two to twelve months or even longer. Octopus mothers die soon after their eggs hatch.
pages.brief: A mother octopus rests beside a cluster of eggs attached to a rock in the ocean. She watches over the eggs, her arms curled protectively around them. Nearby, a few eggs begin to hatch, showing tiny young octopuses after a long wait.

pages.text: What Are Octopuses Like? Octopuses can be big or small. They have two big eyes, a beak, and a soft, round body. They also have eight long arms— each with its own brain! Octopuses have nine brains in total. Near its head, an octopus has a tube called a siphon (SY-fun). An octopus can shoot water, waste, and ink out of its siphon.
pages.brief: A large octopus floats in clear ocean water, showing two big eyes, a small beak and a soft round body. Its eight long arms spread out. Near its head, a siphon releases a stream of water and ink.

pages.text: Do You Know? The arms of octopuses are covered with suckers. They help octopuses move around, grab onto rocks, and catch prey. Suckers also let octopuses taste.
pages.brief: A close view of an octopus arm shows round suckers along its underside. The arm grips a rock while another sucker touches a small fish. The suckers help the octopus hold on, catch prey and taste what it touches in the ocean.

pages.text: Octopuses don’t have any bones. They can fit into small spaces. Octopuses very smart. They can find their way out of a maze and can even use tools.
pages.brief: An octopus squeezes its boneless body through a narrow gap between rocks. Beside it, another octopus moves through a simple maze. Nearby, an octopus holds a small object with its arm, showing that it can use tools.

pages.text: Where Do Octopuses Live? Octopuses usually live in warm water. Some octopuses live in very cold water. Many octopuses like deep ocean waters. Others swim near the ocean’s surface.
pages.brief: Several octopuses live in different parts of the ocean. One drifts in warm, sunlit water near the surface, while another sits in cold, darker water. Far below, an octopus moves through deep ocean water, and another swims close to the surface.

pages.text: How Do Octopuses Move? Octopuses can swim fast in an unusual way. First, they take water into their body. Then, they squirt water out of their siphon. The force pushes octopuses backward. Swimming is hard work for octopuses. It’s easier for them to crawl along the ocean floor.
pages.brief: An octopus takes water into its body, then squirts it out through its siphon. The force pushes the octopus backward through the water. Below, another octopus crawls more easily along the ocean floor, using its arms to pull itself over rocks and sand.

pages.text: How Do Octopuses Hunt and Stay Safe? Octopuses hunt fish, snakes, and other ocean animals. Octopuses drop down on their prey. The prey sticks to their suckers. Then octopuses pull their food into their beak.
pages.brief: An octopus drops down onto prey in the ocean. A fish and a snake stick to the suckers on its arms. The octopus pulls the prey toward its beak, ready to eat, while other small ocean animals swim nearby.

pages.text: Predators of octopuses include whales, seals, and large fish. When predators attack, octopuses have different ways to escape. An octopus can bite an pass on venom.
pages.brief: A whale, a seal and a large fish surround an octopus in the ocean. The octopus opens its beak to bite and pass on venom as it tries to escape. Its arms curl and reach while the predators close in.

pages.text: Octopuses can also shoot dark ink out of their siphon so predators can’t see them.
pages.brief: An octopus shoots a cloud of dark ink from its siphon into the ocean water. The ink spreads around it, hiding the octopus from a nearby predator. The predator peers through the dark cloud, unable to see the octopus clearly.

pages.text: Octopuses can even blend in with the colors around them. Then predators can’t see them. Sometimes octopuses get caught. However, if an octopus loses an arm, it can grow a new one!
pages.brief: An octopus blends in with the colors of the coral and rocks around it, while a predator looks nearby. Another octopus has lost an arm, and a small new arm is growing in its place. Both octopuses stay hidden in the ocean.

pages.text: Conclusion Octopuses can do many things. They can swim backward, shoot ink, change colors, and even grow new arms. Octopuses are amazing animals!
pages.brief: An octopus swims backward through the ocean, then shoots a cloud of dark ink from its siphon. Nearby, an octopus changes color to match the rocks, and another shows a new arm growing where an old one was lost. These actions show how amazing octopuses are.

books.art_why: The book is about real animals that exist today, so photographs suit it.

pages.text: Introduction The world is full of interesting animals. Some animals look strange or have special skills. Let’s look at some of these wonders of nature.
pages.brief: A varied group of interesting animals is shown together, some with strange shapes and some with special skills. The scene presents these animals as wonders of nature, inviting a look at the unusual creatures in the world.

pages.text: Trap-Door Spider The trap-door spider lives in a tunnel in the ground. Its home has a hidden door made of silk and dirt. The spider hides in its tunnel to hunt.
pages.brief: A trap-door spider is inside a tunnel in the ground. Its hidden door is made of silk and dirt. The spider hides in the tunnel as it hunts, and the scene focuses on the spider and its hidden home.

pages.text: Beaver Beavers chew through tree trunks. They make dams out of trees, mud, and stones.
pages.brief: A beaver chews through a tree trunk. Nearby, a dam is made from trees, mud, and stones. The beaver is shown at work with the materials named on the page, focusing on the beaver and its dam.

pages.text: Chameleon Chameleons change color to hide themselves. They even change color to show how they feel.

pages.text: Leaf Insect The body parts of leaf insects look just like leaves. These animals blend in well with real leaves on trees.
pages.brief: A leaf insect is shown with body parts that look just like leaves. It blends in well with real leaves on trees. The scene shows the leaf insect among the leaves, matching the page’s focus on its leaf-like body.

pages.brief: A female leaf-rolling weevil is shown with a leaf shaped into a cone. The page shows her laying the cone, and the leaf is with her eggs. The scene centers on the female weevil, the leaf cone, and the eggs.

pages.text: Praying Mantis The praying mantis holds its front legs in a praying position. A mantis has five eyes to help it hunt for food.
pages.brief: A praying mantis is shown holding its front legs in a praying position. It has five eyes to help it hunt for food. The scene focuses on the mantis, its front legs, and its eyes.

pages.text: Mole Moles dig tunnels to find and eat worms. These animals have tiny eyes, but they are not blind.
pages.brief: A mole is shown digging tunnels to find and eat worms. It has tiny eyes, but it is not blind. The scene focuses on the mole, its tunnels, the worms it finds, and its small eyes.

pages.text: Sea Dragon Sea dragons are small fish. They look like ocean plants. Their leafy parts help them catch food and hide from enemies.
pages.brief: A sea dragon is shown as a small fish that looks like an ocean plant. Its leafy parts help it catch food and hide from enemies. The scene focuses on the sea dragon and its leafy parts.

pages.text: Conclusion Interesting animals come in many shapes and sizes. They are all wonders of nature.
pages.brief: Interesting animals of many shapes and sizes are shown together in the scene. They are all presented as wonders of nature. The scene brings these animals together in a final look at their different forms and sizes.

books.title: Ocean Animals
books.art_why: Ocean animals alive today are best shown with real underwater photography.

pages.text: Many kinds of animals live in the ocean. They are part of the ocean community.
pages.brief: A wide underwater view of the open blue ocean, with several different sea animals of different shapes and sizes swimming at different depths, sunlight filtering down from the surface above them and open water stretching away in every direction.

pages.text: . reptiles, fish, or mammals Most of the ones in this book are Let’s meet some of these ocean animals.
pages.brief: A bright underwater scene showing a mix of ocean animals together in blue water: a fish swimming past, a sea turtle gliding, and a large whale in the distance, presented as examples of the fish, reptiles and mammals that live in the ocean.

pages.text: I am a dolphin. I have a sleek body and a strong tail to swim fast. I live in a group called a pod, and I like to eat fish. I whistle to talk to other dolphins.
pages.brief: A sleek dolphin with smooth skin and a strong tail swims fast through clear blue water, several other dolphins swimming close beside it in a pod, and a small group of fish scattering ahead as the dolphin whistles with its mouth slightly open.

pages.text: My thick layer of fat keeps me warm. I live on ice and in cold water. I use them to dig for clams and to protect myself. I am a walrus, and I have ivory tusks.
pages.brief: A large walrus with long ivory tusks hauls its heavy body up onto floating ice in cold grey water, its thick folds of fat visible, one tusk lowered toward the shallow bottom where it digs for clams in the freezing sea.

pages.text: I am a hammerhead shark, and my head has a very funny shape. My eyes and nostrils are at the ends of lobes. I like to eat fish.
pages.brief: A hammerhead shark swims through blue water, its wide flat head stretched out sideways with the eyes and nostrils set at the far ends of the lobes, a school of small fish swimming just ahead of its open mouth.

pages.text: I eat squid, octopus, and fish. I bark like a dog, and I am covered by short fur. I am smart, noisy, and playful. I am a California sea lion.
pages.brief: A California sea lion with short brown fur swims and twists in bright coastal water, mouth open as it barks, front flippers pushing it along, a squid and small fish nearby in the water around it, its playful body tilted mid-roll.

pages.text: I am an octopus. I have a soft body and no skeleton. I have eight arms with suckers. I shoot black ink from my body to hide and escape from danger. I can also change the color of my skin.
pages.brief: An octopus with a soft boneless body rests among rocks in blue water, its eight sucker-covered arms curling outward, a cloud of black ink spreading behind it while its skin shifts from pale to deep red.

pages.text: I eat seals, dolphins, and fish. that are shaped like triangles. I have very sharp teeth I am a large and fierce shark. I am a great white shark.
pages.brief: A huge great white shark cruises through clear blue water, rows of sharp triangular teeth showing in its open mouth, its eye fixed on a seal swimming above near the sunlit surface.

pages.text: I am a manta ray. I have fins that look like wings. I am related to stingrays, but I do not sting.
pages.brief: A manta ray glides through open blue water, its wide fins moving like slow wings, casting a shadow over the sandy sea floor far below while small fish drift around its broad flat body.

pages.text: Male sea horses, favorite food. Shrimp are my to hide. I change color I am a fish. a horse. but I am not I am a sea horse, carry eggs until they hatch.
pages.brief: A sea horse hovers among green seagrass in shallow water, its curled tail gripping a blade of weed, its colour shifting to match the plants, tiny shrimp drifting nearby and a pouch on the male's belly holding eggs.

pages.text: I am a leatherback turtle, the biggest turtle in the world. I lay eggs on land. Jellyfish are my favorite food. I am covered with leathery skin instead of a shell.
pages.brief: A leatherback turtle, the biggest turtle in the world, swims through blue water with long front flippers, its leathery skin ridged instead of a hard shell, a jellyfish drifting just ahead; on a sandy shore behind, a nest of eggs lies in the sand.

pages.text: I eat tiny animals called krill. I make deep sounds that move through water. I am the largest mammal ever to live. I am a blue whale.
pages.brief: An enormous blue whale swims through deep open ocean, its huge mouth open as it takes in a cloud of tiny krill, its long body filling the frame while faint ripples of sound spread through the surrounding water.

pages.text: The ocean is home to all these animals. Many of them are endangered. They all suffer because of pollution and hunting. Keeping our oceans clean will help keep these animals alive.
pages.brief: A wide ocean scene showing many of the animals from the book together in blue water, dolphin, shark, turtle, whale and sea lion, with drifting rubbish and pollution in the water around them and clean open sea beyond.

books.title: Firefighters
books.art_why: Firefighters, fire trucks, fireboats and helicopters are real today and are regularly photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Have you ever heard a fire truck racing to a fire? Firefighters put out fires and save lives. They help keep fires from starting. They teach people about fire safety.
pages.brief: A bright red fire truck races along a city street with lights flashing, while nearby a firefighter in full gear kneels to talk with a small group of children and their parents about fire safety, showing them how to stay safe at home.

pages.text: What Makes Fire Burn Fires need air to burn. They also need fuel. Wood and oil are two kinds of fuel. The more fuel, the hotter the fire will be. But even a candle flame burns very hot. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A close view of a candle burning with a tall orange flame, beside split logs of wood and a small can of oil. Clear air surrounds the flame, showing that fire needs air and fuel to keep burning and that more fuel makes a hotter fire.

pages.text: Kinds of Fires Firefighters put out fires in houses and tall buildings. They also fight forest fires. They must be ready to put out many kinds of fires.
pages.brief: Three scenes of firefighting: firefighters spraying a house fire, firefighters climbing inside a tall building, and a line of firefighters working against a forest fire among trees and smoke on a hillside.

pages.text: Firefighting Tools Firefighters use many different tools. spray They use hoses to water or foam on fires. They break down doors with axes. They use ladders to reach high places.
pages.brief: Firefighters at a fire scene use their tools: one aims a thick hose spraying water and foam, another swings an axe to break down a door, and a third climbs a ladder propped against a high wall.

pages.text: Smoke masks protect firefighters from smoke. Fans move smoke from rooms. Fire extinguishers can put out small fires.
pages.brief: Inside a smoky room, a firefighter wears a smoke mask over the face, a large fan blows smoke out through a doorway, and a firefighter lifts a small red fire extinguisher toward a small fire.

pages.text: Firefighting Machines Fire trucks are important firefighting machines. A fire engine has a pump to spray water.
pages.brief: A red fire engine parked on a street with its side panels open, showing the pump and hoses. A firefighter stands beside it working the pump to spray water toward a fire in the distance.

pages.text: Ladder trucks carry ladders. Tanker trucks carry water. Rescue trucks carry tools to help trapped people.
pages.brief: Three trucks side by side at a station: a ladder truck with long ladders on top, a tanker truck carrying water, and a rescue truck loaded with tools for helping trapped people.

pages.text: Other kinds of machines fight fires, too. Fireboats fight fires from the water. Helicopters drop water on fires. Planes help put out forest fires, too.
pages.brief: A fireboat on the water spraying streams at a fire on a waterfront, a helicopter overhead dropping water from a bucket, and a plane flying low over a forest releasing water on the trees.

pages.text: Becoming a Firefighter Firefighters must be at least eighteen years old. They must be strong and in good shape. They must also pass a written test.
pages.brief: Young adult firefighters at a training ground, strong and in good shape, climbing, lifting and running through drills, while one sits at a table writing a written test with a pencil.

pages.text: Firefighters go to school for training. They learn how to fight different kinds of fires. They also learn how to treat hurt people.
pages.brief: Firefighter trainees in a classroom and practice yard at school, learning to fight different kinds of fires with hoses and extinguishers, and practicing how to treat a hurt person lying on a mat.

pages.text: Conclusion Fire is useful, of course. People have used it to cook and stay warm for many thousands of years. At the same time, fire can be very dangerous. Fires take many lives and destroy forests.
pages.brief: A family cooks food over a campfire and warms their hands by a fireplace, then the same page shows a dangerous wildfire burning through a forest, flames and smoke rising among the trees.

pages.text: Fires also destroy thousands of buildings every year. Long ago, fires burned down entire cities. Today, firefighters put out fires and keep us safe.
pages.brief: A burned building standing in a modern city with firefighters spraying water on it, and beside that an old drawing-like scene of an entire old city street on fire long ago, buildings burning.

books.title: Garrett Morgan and the Traffic Signal
books.art_why: Garrett Morgan is a named famous person, and the book tells his story.

pages.text: Traffic Problems In the 1920s, the streets were getting very busy. Many things shared the streets.
pages.brief: A wide city street in the 1920s is crowded with many kinds of traffic sharing the same road. Different vehicles and travelers move along the busy street at once, filling the roadway from side to side as they all try to get where they are going.

pages.text: Cars were on the streets. Horses and buggies were on the streets. People and bikes were on the streets, too.
pages.brief: On the city street, cars roll along beside horses pulling buggies. People walk and bicycles ride among them, all sharing the roadway. The street is full of mixed traffic moving in different directions at the same time.

pages.text: A man named Garrett Morgan lived in Cleveland, Ohio. He saw a car on the street hit a horse and buggy. He saw that the streets were not safe.
pages.brief: In Cleveland, Ohio, a man named Garrett Morgan stands on the street and watches as a car hits a horse and buggy. He sees the crash happen in front of him and understands that the streets are not safe.

pages.text: Making a Plan Each day more traffic was on the streets. Mr. Morgan knew there would be more traffic problems. He thought about how to solve these problems.
pages.brief: Each day more traffic fills the streets of Cleveland. Mr. Morgan watches the growing crowds of vehicles and knows there will be more traffic problems. He thinks hard about how to solve these problems before they get worse.

pages.text: Mr. Morgan knew Cleveland needed a way to help the traffic. He thought about how to do this. He made a plan for a traffic signal.
pages.brief: Mr. Morgan knows Cleveland needs a way to help the traffic move safely. He thinks carefully about how to do this, then makes a plan for a traffic signal that could control the traffic on the streets.

pages.text: The Traffic Signal The traffic signal had arms. The arms went up and down.
pages.brief: The traffic signal Mr. Morgan planned has arms that go up and down. The signal stands at the street, and its moving arms show traffic when to stop and when to go, helping the traffic move in an orderly way.

pages.text: Later, traffic signals used lights. The lights told traffic when to stop and when to go.
pages.brief: Later, traffic signals use lights instead of arms. The lights glow at the street and tell traffic when to stop and when to go, so drivers and people know what to do at the crossing.

pages.text: Mr. Morgan’s traffic signal could also stop all traffic. Then it was safe for people to cross the street.
pages.brief: Mr. Morgan's traffic signal can also stop all traffic at once. When all the traffic stops, it is safe for people to cross the street, and they can walk across without cars, horses, or bikes moving through.

pages.text: The traffic signal was put on street corners. It was easy to make traffic stop and go at corners. Mr. Morgan’s plan worked!
pages.brief: The traffic signal is put up on street corners. At the corners it is easy to make traffic stop and go, and the signal helps keep the traffic moving safely. Mr. Morgan's plan works, and the corners are busy but orderly.

pages.text: The Man with the Plan Garrett Morgan made the streets safe for people, cars, and horses and buggies.
pages.brief: Garrett Morgan has made the streets safe for people, cars, and horses and buggies. The busy street is now orderly, with all the different kinds of traffic sharing the road safely because of his traffic signal.

pages.text: Mr. Morgan also made other things. He made a mask to help keep firefighters safe. He also started a newspaper in Cleveland.
pages.brief: Mr. Morgan also makes other things. He makes a mask that helps keep firefighters safe while they work. He also starts a newspaper in Cleveland, showing that he has many ideas and works to help people in different ways.

pages.text: Mr. Morgan was a problem solver. He saw a problem. He looked for a way to solve it.
pages.brief: Mr. Morgan is a problem solver. He sees a problem on the streets, then he looks for a way to solve it. He thinks about the problem and works out a plan, just as he did with the traffic signal.

books.title: What Pet Should You Get?
books.art_why: Real pets and children can be shown in real photographs.

pages.text: Introduction Almost every kid has wanted to have a pet. Pets can make good friends. But how do you decide which kind of pet to get?
pages.brief: A young child stands in a room, thinking about having a pet. A friendly pet sits nearby. The child looks curious and thoughtful, considering what kind of animal could become a good friend and how to decide.

pages.text: Here are some kids who have some opinions about pets. Read what they have to say. Then decide what kind of pet you would like to have.
pages.brief: Several kids gather together, each sharing an opinion about pets. They look at one another and gesture as they talk. Their faces show different feelings, from excited to doubtful, as they think about choosing a pet.

pages.text: Dogs as Pets Every kid should own a dog. A dog comes when you call it. You know it likes you because it wags its tail. Dogs like to play chase with you. Some dogs will even play catch! Get a dog for a great playmate!
pages.brief: A child calls a dog in a yard. The dog runs over, wagging its tail. The child and dog play chase, then play catch with a ball. The dog looks happy and eager as a playful companion.

pages.text: Dogs as Pets Dogs are hard pets to keep. They need lots of space to run. What if you don’t have a yard? You have to take them on walks even if it is cold. The worst thing is that you have to clean up after them. Yuck, who wants a dog?
pages.brief: A dog runs in a small space without a yard. A child walks the dog outside in cold weather, bundled up. Later, the child carefully cleans up after the dog, looking unhappy at the messy job.

pages.text: Lizards as Pets Lizards make the coolest pets. They don’t bark or meow. You don’t have to take them for walks. They are easy to hold and to pet. It doesn’t cost much for lizard food. So, go get a lizard!
pages.brief: A child gently holds a calm lizard in both hands. The lizard rests easily, and the child strokes its back. A small dish of lizard food sits close by, showing that feeding it does not cost much.

pages.text: Lizards as Pets It is mean to keep lizards as pets. Some have to stay in one tiny box their whole life. Some of them eat live crickets. Plus, it feels really weird to pet them. Never, ever, get a lizard!
pages.brief: A lizard sits inside a tiny box-like enclosure. Nearby, live crickets crawl in a container. A child reaches toward the lizard, then pulls back with a hesitant, uncomfortable face, showing that petting it feels strange.

pages.text: Fish as Pets Fish make awesome pets. They come in such pretty colors. It is fun to watch them swim back and forth. It is fun to watch their funny mouths. They only need to be fed once a day. Fish make fun and easy pets to keep.
pages.brief: Colorful fish swim back and forth inside a clear aquarium. A child watches closely, smiling at the fish’s funny mouths. A small amount of food is sprinkled in once, showing the fish only need one feeding a day.

pages.text: Fish as Pets Fish should be left in the oceans and rivers. Fish don’t come when you call them. They can’t do any tricks. And worse than that, fish don’t like to be touched. Fish win the most boring pet award.
pages.brief: Fish swim freely in a wide river or ocean. A child stands on the bank, watching but not touching them. The fish do not come when called and do not perform tricks, making them seem boring as pets.

pages.text: Parrots as Pets One of the best pets to own is a parrot. Parrots are very beautiful birds. They often do not need a cage. I love it when my parrot says “hello.” Some parrots even whistle. Get a parrot and teach it to talk.
pages.brief: A beautiful parrot perches on a child’s arm, not inside a cage. The parrot opens its beak and says “hello.” The child smiles and listens closely, then gently points as if ready to teach the parrot to talk.

pages.text: Parrots as Pets Parrots are really messy pets. They spill seeds and fruit all over. They are not the best drinkers. They get water on the floor. Their feathers can even fall out. Don’t get a parrot unless you like cleaning!
pages.brief: A parrot makes a mess, spilling seeds and fruit pieces around. Water splashes onto the floor from its drinking cup because it is not a neat drinker. Loose feathers drift down. A child cleans the messy floor, looking tired but determined.

pages.text: Conclusion There are good things and bad things about each pet. You have to decide whether the good things are great. You have to decide whether the bad things are okay for you.
pages.brief: A child sits thoughtfully, considering different pets and weighing good points against bad ones. The child’s face shows careful thinking, as if deciding whether each pet’s good things are great and its bad things are okay.

pages.text: You also have to do research to see whether your house is good for a pet. Don’t get a pet unless you have thought hard about it. But the right pet can be your best friend!
pages.brief: A child and an adult look around a home, checking whether it is a good place for a pet. They consider space and care needs together. The child looks serious and thoughtful, ready to think hard before choosing the right pet.
